title: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027
official_title: To authorize appropriations for fiscal year 2027 for military activities of the Department of Defense, for military construction, and for defense activities of the Department of Energy, to prescribe military personnel strengths for such fiscal year, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: The annual NDAA has been enacted into law every fiscal year for more than six consecutive decades. This House-passed version was introduced by House Armed Services Chairman Rogers (R-AL-3) with Ranking Member Smith (D-WA-9) as an original cosponsor, and cleared the House on July 22, 2026. Remaining variables are Senate committee markup, floor amendments in either chamber, and the conference-committee outcome on the more contested provisions — Section 1655 space-based interceptors, Section 1246 Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative funding, Sections 1221-1223 Israel cooperation extensions, Section 1237 NATO burden-sharing reports, and Section 1247 Korean Peninsula posture funding limits. None of those disputes have historically been large enough to prevent an NDAA from being enacted before the fiscal year ends.
summary: This is the annual defense authorization bill for fiscal year 2027, organized into four divisions covering the Department of Defense, military construction, Department of Energy defense-related programs, and the funding tables that give effect to the authorizations. Section 401 sets active-duty end strengths of 469,000 Army; 356,600 Navy; 173,700 Marine Corps; 330,400 Air Force; and 13,200 Space Force. Division B authorizes named military construction projects by service branch — Army, Navy, Air Force, Defense Agencies, and NATO Security Investment Program — plus separate Guard and Reserve construction authorizations. On the personnel side, Section 632 raises the death gratuity payable to survivors from $100,000 to $165,000 with annual Consumer Price Index adjustment beginning January 1, 2027, and Section 706 requires TRICARE to cover up to a 365-day supply of contraception on the uniform formulary. Foreign-policy items include a Section 1246 authorization of up to $1.00B for the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative, Section 1221 extension of the Israel war reserve stockpile authority through January 1, 2029, and Section 1237 quarterly NATO burden-sharing reports evaluating allied progress toward the 5 percent defense investment commitment agreed at the 2025 Hague Summit. Division C Section 3501 authorizes $873.5M for the U.S. Merchant Marine Academy and separately funds the Maritime Security Program ($400.5M), Tanker Security Fleet ($167.6M), Cable Security Fleet ($30M), port infrastructure ($550M), small shipyards ($105M), and other Maritime Administration programs.
brief: The FY2027 defense authorization bill — sets DoD/DOE-defense/military construction spending ceilings, personnel end strengths, and dozens of policy provisions from Taiwan and Israel cooperation to a new AI Model Rapid Deployment Framework and a $1.97B-plus military construction program.

top_lines.headline: Authorizes FY2027 DoD Spending Levels and Sets Force Sizes
subs: Sections 101, 201, 301, and 421 authorize appropriations for procurement, research/development/test/evaluation, operation and maintenance, and military personnel — with the specific dollar amounts set out in the Division D funding tables (Sections 4101, 4201, 4301, 4401)
Section 401 sets active-duty end strengths as of September 30, 2027: Army 469,000; Navy 356,600; Marine Corps 173,700; Air Force 330,400; Space Force 13,200

Section 411 sets Selected Reserve strengths: Army National Guard 331,300; Army Reserve 172,000; Navy Reserve 56,500; Marine Corps Reserve 34,700; Air National Guard 107,400; Air Force Reserve 67,400; Coast Guard Reserve 8,500
Section 1001 provides $6.00B in general transfer authority letting the Secretary of Defense move funds between accounts within the authorization

top_lines.headline: Military Construction Across the Services
subs: Section 2101 authorizes $1.97B for Army construction and land acquisition (10 items)
Section 2201 authorizes $19.25B for Navy construction and land acquisition (18 items)
Section 2301 authorizes $9.94B for Air Force construction and land acquisition (30 items)
Section 2401 authorizes $5.24B for Defense Agencies construction and land acquisition (21 items), plus Section 2402 authorizes $694.3M for the Energy Resilience and Conservation Investment Program
Section 2501 authorizes $604.3M for NATO Security Investment Program construction projects

top_lines.headline: Servicemember Pay, Benefits, and Family Provisions
subs: Section 632 raises the death gratuity payable to survivors of a servicemember killed on active duty from $100,000 to $165,000, applicable to deaths on or after enactment, and adds a Consumer Price Index cost-of-living adjustment beginning January 1, 2027

Section 706 requires TRICARE to cover a supply of up to 365 days of a contraceptive on the uniform formulary — including in a single fill or refill — for members on active duty and their dependents, starting no later than 180 days after enactment

Section 612 makes permanent the Secretary concerned's authority under 37 USC 403 to authorize temporary Basic Allowance for Housing increases in areas covered by a major disaster declaration, experiencing an influx of military personnel, or where actual housing costs exceed current BAH rates by more than 20 percent, by striking the sunset subparagraphs in 37 USC 403(b)(7) and (b)(8)
Section 615 authorizes the Department to pay the cost of shipping breast milk for a servicemember mother performing duty away from her nursing child
Section 601 extends most expiring bonus, incentive-pay, and special-pay authorities from December 31, 2026 to December 31, 2027

top_lines.headline: Foreign-Policy Provisions: Israel, Taiwan, NATO, China, Korea
subs: Section 1246 authorizes up to $1.00B for the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative for fiscal year 2027

Section 1221 extends the U.S. war reserve stockpile authority for Israel from January 1, 2027 to January 1, 2029; Section 1222 renames the U.S.-Israel anti-tunnel cooperation program "subterranean" and extends it through 2029; Section 1223 extends U.S.-Israel counter-unmanned-systems cooperation through 2029

Section 1237 requires the U.S. European Command Commander to submit 90-day reports through January 1, 2028 on allied progress toward the 5 percent defense-investment commitment agreed at the 2025 Hague NATO Summit, and on force posture and readiness on NATO's eastern flank

Section 1247 extends existing restrictions on obligating or expending U.S. funds for changes to U.S. military posture on the Korean Peninsula to cover fiscal year 2027 amounts as well as fiscal year 2026
Section 1722 requires a classified report on Russian and Chinese intelligence penetration in Georgia, plus a 5-year State Department strategy for bilateral relations with Georgia

top_lines.headline: Emerging Technology and Missile-Defense Provisions
subs: Section 1523 directs the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer to establish an AI Model Rapid Deployment Framework, with the objective of deploying artificial intelligence systems on Department enterprise AI platforms within 30 days after public availability

Section 1655 requires the Director of Cost Assessment and Program Evaluation to conduct an independent life-cycle cost estimate of the space-based interceptor program, and bars a full-rate production contract until the Secretary certifies at least one successful operationally relevant flight test
Section 1656 directs the Missile Defense Agency to develop and demonstrate a low-cost exo-atmospheric interceptor complementary to existing ballistic-missile-defense interceptors

Section 3111 rewrites 10 USC 6128(a) to require the Department of Energy to ensure the nuclear security enterprise has the capability to reliably produce no fewer than 180 war reserve plutonium pits annually by not later than 2050

Section 1811 requires annual reports through 2032 on supply-chain dependencies for biotechnology equipment and services, including a classified annex identifying any biotechnology company of concern being considered for OMB designation

items.main: Titles I through XVIII cover procurement, research-and-development, operation and maintenance, military personnel, personnel policy, compensation, health care, acquisition policy, DoD organization, general provisions, civilian personnel, foreign nations, other authorizations, cyberspace, space and strategic programs, other defense matters, and revitalization of the defense industrial base.
items.detail: The dollar amounts for procurement, RDT&E, O&M, military personnel, and other authorizations are set out in the Division D funding tables under Sections 4101, 4201, 4301, 4401, and 4501, incorporated by reference under Section 4001. Section 1001 authorizes the Secretary of Defense to transfer up to $6.00B between accounts within the authorization, subject to notification requirements.

items.main: Includes numerous authorities on specific weapon systems: Section 123 authorizes a multiyear procurement contract for up to 15 Arleigh Burke Flight III destroyers; Section 124 authorizes multiyear procurement for John Lewis class oilers; Section 127 authorizes multiyear procurement for E-2D Advanced Hawkeye aircraft; Section 128 authorizes incremental funding for ship-to-shore connector construction.
items.detail: Section 123(e) caps modifications to the destroyer multiyear contract at 10 percent above the original target price. Section 123(d) requires that if fewer than 15 destroyers are procured through the base contracts, one or more contracts must include a prepriced option so the base plus option quantity reaches 15. Section 122 gives the Navy incremental funding authority for long-lead components on Virginia class submarines.

items.main: Section 142 extends the existing statutory prohibition on retiring F-22 aircraft; Sections 143, 145, 146, and 147 impose or extend limitations on retirement or availability of E-3 AWACS, C-130, C-37, and MQ-9 Reaper aircraft.
items.detail: Section 144 requires the Air Force to evaluate the potential transfer of certain A-10 aircraft. Section 141 sets minimum inventory requirements for certain fighter aircraft. These provisions constrain the services' ability to divest older platforms during FY2027.

items.main: Authorizes named construction and land-acquisition projects at specific installations by service branch — $1.97B Army (Section 2101), $19.25B Navy (Section 2201), $9.94B Air Force (Section 2301), $5.24B Defense Agencies (Section 2401), $604.3M NATO Security Investment Program (Section 2501), plus $694.3M for the Energy Resilience and Conservation Investment Program (Section 2402).
items.detail: Guard and Reserve construction is authorized separately under Sections 2601-2605: Army National Guard $225.5M, Army Reserve $178.0M, Navy Reserve and Marine Corps Reserve $47.0M, Air National Guard $531.0M, Air Force Reserve $19.5M. Sections 2511 and 2512 authorize $416.5M in Republic of Korea funded projects and $134.0M in Republic of Poland funded projects.

items.main: Extends the authority to carry out named military construction projects authorized in prior fiscal years but not yet completed — Section 2108 extends fiscal-year projects with a $656.4M summed value across 11 items; Section 2205 extends Navy projects with a $2.43B summed value across 14 items; Section 2307 extends Air Force projects with a $1.31B summed value across 19 items; Section 2405 extends Defense Agencies projects with a $555.4M summed value across 12 items.
items.detail: Section 2607 and Section 2608 similarly extend Guard and Reserve project authorities with summed values of $323.7M and $349.9M respectively. Section 2802 adds Tribal governments to the list of entities eligible for defense community infrastructure program grants. Section 2804 raises unspecified minor military construction dollar thresholds.

sections.label: Division C — DOE Defense Programs and Maritime (Titles XXXI–XXXVI)

items.main: Section 3101 authorizes the Department of Energy's National Nuclear Security Administration activities for fiscal year 2027 per the funding table in Section 4701, and specifically authorizes a new $88.7M Plutonium Engineering Support Building at Los Alamos National Laboratory.
items.detail: Section 3102 authorizes defense environmental cleanup, Section 3103 authorizes other defense activities, and Section 3104 authorizes nuclear energy — all per the Section 4701 funding table. Section 3111 rewrites 10 USC 6128(a) to set the plutonium pit production capability requirement at 180 pits annually by not later than 2050, and shifts the pit-production report from annual to "each odd numbered year." Section 3112 changes the federal cost share for accelerating replacement of cesium blood irradiation sources from 50 percent to 100 percent of the per-device cost.

items.main: Section 3501 authorizes $873.5M for the U.S. Merchant Marine Academy in fiscal year 2027 — of which $129.5M is for Academy operations, $120M is for facilities and infrastructure under the Campus Modernization Plan, and $624M is for capital improvement projects.
items.detail: Section 3501 also authorizes $53.4M for State maritime academies (including $9.4M for the Student Incentive Payment Program), $75M for the National Security Multi-Mission Vessel program, $105.76M for Maritime Administration operations, $6M for disposal of obsolete vessels, $400.5M for the Maritime Security Program, $30M for the Cable Security Fleet, $167.6M for the Tanker Security Fleet, $33.7M for the Federal Ship Financing Program (Title XI loan guarantees), $105M for the Small Shipyards Program, $550M for the Port Infrastructure Development Program, and $300M in maritime incentive payments to designated centers of excellence. Section 3531 requires the President to submit implementation proposals for the February 2026 White House Maritime Action Plan within 90 days of enactment.

underreported.summary: Section 3111 sets a 2050 target date for the Department of Energy's plutonium-pit production capability of 180 pits per year — a long-horizon commitment on a key nuclear-weapons enterprise metric that receives little coverage compared with weapon-system authorizations.
underreported.why_unreported: Plutonium pit production capacity is a technical nuclear-enterprise milestone rather than a headline weapon system, and the bill also downshifts the associated report from annual to every other year, further reducing the frequency at which the milestone gets public attention.

underreported.summary: Section 1655 imposes hard gates on the space-based interceptor program — no full-rate production contract until the Director of Cost Assessment and Program Evaluation completes an independent life-cycle cost estimate, and no full-rate production decision until at least one successful operationally relevant flight test has occurred.
underreported.why_unreported: The public debate over space-based interceptors focuses on whether to pursue them at all, so procedural cost-and-test gates that constrain how quickly the Missile Defense Agency can move the program to production tend to be overlooked.

underreported.summary: Section 3501 authorizes a broad slate of Maritime Administration programs — Merchant Marine Academy, State maritime academies, Maritime Security Program, Tanker Security Fleet, Cable Security Fleet, port infrastructure, small shipyards, and centers of excellence — inside a defense authorization bill rather than a transportation or maritime bill.
underreported.why_unreported: The Maritime Administration is a Department of Transportation agency, not a DoD component, so its authorization being packaged in the NDAA as Division C, Title XXXV places substantial DOT program funding outside the visibility of most transportation-policy coverage.

new: Section 1523 creates a new Artificial Intelligence Model Rapid Deployment Framework at the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer, targeting a 30-day deployment window for AI systems onto Department enterprise AI platforms after public availability.

Section 1811 establishes annual reports through 2032 identifying supply-chain dependencies for biotechnology equipment and services obtained by the Department of Defense, with a classified annex identifying covered foreign entities being considered for biotechnology-company-of-concern designation.

Section 3113 creates new Other Transaction Authority for the National Nuclear Security Administration Administrator, adapting the DoD Section 4021/4022 acquisition authorities for the nuclear security enterprise.
Section 3531 requires the President to submit implementation proposals for the February 2026 White House Maritime Action Plan within 90 days of enactment.
modified: Section 632 raises the death gratuity from $100,000 to $165,000 and adds a permanent Consumer Price Index annual adjustment beginning January 1, 2027.

Section 706 expands the TRICARE contraceptive benefit to include a single-fill or refill supply of up to 365 days at military pharmacies, retail network pharmacies, and the national mail-order pharmacy.
Section 1246 modifies the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative to authorize up to $1.00B of the fiscal-year-2027 DoD authorization for the initiative's purposes.
Section 1221 extends the Israel war reserve stockpile authority under Section 12001(d) of the 2005 DoD Appropriations Act from January 1, 2027 to January 1, 2029.

Section 3111 rewrites 10 USC 6128(a) to set the plutonium-pit production-capability requirement at 180 pits annually by not later than 2050, and shifts the associated congressional report from annual to every other year.
Section 3112 raises the federal cost share for replacing cesium blood irradiation sources from 50 percent to 100 percent of the per-device cost.

gaps: The bill does not itself set the FY2027 basic-pay-raise percentage — that adjustment continues to be governed by the annual Employment Cost Index formula under 37 USC 1009 absent a specific NDAA override.
The bill authorizes appropriations but does not itself appropriate money — actual funding flows through a separate Defense Appropriations Act that must clear both chambers.

The bill contains no free-standing policy on Ukraine security assistance, and no provisions specifically addressing operations at the southern border, both of which have been contested topics in prior NDAAs.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Wittman
featured_quotes.text: I rise in strong support today of H.R. 8800, the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027. Also, I thank our Tactical Air and Land professional staff: Michael Kirlin, Heath Bope, Caroline Kehrli, Brooke Alred, Amelia Litynski, Jay Vallario, and Andrew Smith. The FY27 NDAA takes several steps to ensure that our servicemembers operate with unmatched capabilities to deter and defeat any adversaries. This bill allows the Secretary of War to enter into multiyear procurement contracts for both the F-15EX and F-35 aircraft.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Jackson
featured_quotes.text: As chairman of the Subcommittee on Intelligence and Special Operations, I am especially proud that this bill provides our Special Operations Forces, the Defense Intelligence Enterprise, and the Security Cooperation Enterprise with the tools and resources needed to execute the Department's National Defense Strategy and counter an ever- changing threat landscape. Crucially, this bill provides an approximately $1.3 billion increase in funding for U.S. Special Operations Command to address critical needs within its programs.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Courtney
featured_quotes.text: As ranking member of the Subcommittee on Seapower and Projection Forces, I yield myself 2\1/4\ minutes. Mr. Chairman, I rise to endorse many provisions of the Seapower and Projections Forces mark of the 2027 NDAA, which our subcommittee crafted under the able leadership of my good friend, Chairman Trent Kelly.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Bacon
featured_quotes.text: By the way, it passed with a huge bipartisan majority in committee. As we have seen across modern battlefields, technology is evolving at a faster rate than ever before. Artificial intelligence, cyber, quantum, biotechnology, and other emerging capabilities are changing the way wars are fought and won. The United States is the gold standard for scientific innovation, and it is of the utmost importance that we remain committed to equipping our servicemembers with the most up-to-date, state-of-the-art, and mission-relevant tools available.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Houlahan
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Chair, today, I have the opportunity to speak briefly with regards to the fiscal year 2027 NDAA. The bipartisan bill that passed out of committee includes many quality-of-life provisions and priorities for our servicemembers and their families. These issues have an immeasurable impact on our recruitment and our retention efforts as well as on readiness. The bill includes a targeted pay raise in which junior servicemembers would get higher pay increases.
